title: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability

learn.hook: Before a cricket match the captains toss a coin. Heads or tails? Nobody knows for sure, but maths can still say how likely each one is!
points: A random experiment is an action whose result cannot be predicted for certain, like tossing a coin or rolling a die.
Each possible result is an outcome. The list of all outcomes is the sample space: rolling a die gives {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
An event is a collection of outcomes, such as 'getting an even number' = {2, 4, 6}.
When all outcomes are equally likely, P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of outcomes.
Every probability lies from 0 to 1. A sure event has probability 1; an impossible event has probability 0.

example.q: A die is rolled once. Find the probability of getting a number greater than 4.

learn.reallife: Ludo, snakes and ladders and the cricket toss are all random experiments. Fair dice and coins make the game fair for everyone.

games.title: How many outcomes?
pairs: Pick a day of the week
Pick a month of the year

quiz.q: How many outcomes are in the sample space when a die is rolled once?
quiz.explain: The die can show 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6: six outcomes.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the number of outcomes with the number of rolls

quiz.q: Two coins are tossed together. How many outcomes are there?
quiz.explain: The outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. HT and TH are different because the coins are different.
quiz.mistake: Counts 'one head and one tail' only once, getting 3

quiz.q: Which event is impossible?
options: Getting an odd number on a die
Getting a head on a coin
Getting a number less than 3 on a die
quiz.explain: A normal die only has 1 to 6, so 7 can never come up. Its probability is 0.
quiz.mistake: Confuses an unlikely event with an impossible one

quiz.q: Which number can NOT be a probability?
quiz.explain: A probability is always between 0 and 1, including 0 and 1. 1.2 is more than 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks probabilities can be bigger than 1

quiz.q: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue balls of the same size. One ball is picked without looking. What is P(red)?
quiz.explain: There are 3 + 5 = 8 equally likely balls, and 3 of them are red. P(red) = 3/8.
quiz.mistake: Divides red by blue (3/5) instead of red by the total

quiz.q: A spinner has 4 equal parts coloured red, blue, green and yellow. What is the probability that it does NOT stop on red?
quiz.explain: Three of the four equal parts are not red, so P(not red) = 3/4.
quiz.mistake: Gives P(red) instead of P(not red)

quiz.q: A die is rolled. How many outcomes are in the event 'getting a prime number'?
quiz.explain: The primes from 1 to 6 are 2, 3 and 5. The number 1 is not prime.
quiz.mistake: Counts 1 as a prime number, getting 4

quiz.q: Two coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting exactly one head?
quiz.explain: Of the 4 outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT, two (HT and TH) have exactly one head. P = 2/4 = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks there are only 3 outcomes, so gives 1/3

teach.ask: Gappu holds a die: "What does it mean to say the chance of rolling a 6 is 1/6?"
teach.praise: There are 6 equally likely outcomes and only 1 of them is a 6, so the chance is 1 out of 6. Now I understand dice!
teach.nudge: How many different results can the die show, and are they all equally likely?

learn.hook: Toss a coin 10 times and you might get 7 heads. Toss it 1000 times and the share of heads creeps very close to one half. Let's see why!
points: Experimental (empirical) probability is found by actually doing an experiment many times.
P(E) = number of trials in which E happened ÷ total number of trials.
Different runs of the same experiment can give slightly different results.
As the number of trials grows, the experimental probability usually gets closer to the theoretical probability.
The experimental probabilities of all the outcomes add up to 1, so P(not E) = 1 − P(E).

example.q: Kabir tosses a coin 50 times and gets 28 heads. Find the experimental probability of heads and of tails.

learn.reallife: Weather offices say there is a 70% chance of rain because, on past days with similar conditions, it rained on about 70 out of 100 of them.

items.q: 36 of 120 students walk to school: P(walks)?

games.title: What do experiments tell us?
items: If you repeat an experiment, you always get exactly the same probability
Random results change from run to run, so the experimental probability can change too.
More trials usually give an experimental probability closer to the theoretical value
Over many trials the lucky and unlucky runs balance out.
An experimental probability of 0.4 means the event happened in 40% of the trials
Getting 7 heads in 10 tosses proves the coin is unfair
With so few tosses, 7 heads can happen by chance with a fair coin.
Experimental probabilities of all outcomes add up to 1
Every trial gives exactly one outcome, so the counts add up to the total number of trials.

quiz.q: A coin is tossed 200 times and shows heads 112 times. What is the experimental probability of heads?
quiz.mistake: Uses the theoretical value 0.5 instead of the data

quiz.q: A die is rolled 60 times and a 6 appears 12 times. What is the experimental probability of getting a 6?
quiz.explain: P(6) = 12 ÷ 60 = 1/5. The theoretical value 1/6 is close but not the same.
quiz.mistake: Writes the theoretical probability 1/6 instead of using the experiment's data

quiz.q: In a survey of 40 students, 14 said cricket is their favourite sport. What is the probability that a student picked at random from them likes cricket most?
quiz.mistake: Divides by the number who do not like cricket (26) instead of the total

quiz.q: Harpreet scored 50 or more in 5 of her last 25 matches. What is the experimental probability that she scores 50 or more in a match?
quiz.mistake: Divides 25 by 5, or reads 5 as 0.5

quiz.q: A shop checks 500 bulbs and finds 20 defective. What is the probability that a bulb picked at random is NOT defective?
quiz.explain: Good bulbs = 500 − 20 = 480, so P(not defective) = 480 ÷ 500 = 0.96.
quiz.mistake: Gives P(defective) = 0.04 instead

quiz.q: Aisha rolled a die 30 times: 1 came 4 times, 2 came 6 times, 3 came 5 times, 4 came 3 times, 5 came 7 times and 6 came 5 times. What is the experimental probability of getting a 5?
quiz.explain: 5 came 7 times out of 30 rolls, so P(5) = 7/30.
quiz.mistake: Uses the theoretical 1/6, or divides by the other rolls (23)

quiz.q: Which statement about experimental probability is true?
options: It is always exactly equal to the theoretical probability
It can change when the experiment is repeated
quiz.explain: It comes from actual results, which vary from one run of trials to the next.
quiz.mistake: Thinks experimental and theoretical probability are always the same

quiz.q: From past records, the experimental probability of rain on a July day in a town is 0.35. What is the probability of no rain?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts wrongly or adds instead of subtracting

teach.ask: Gappu tossed a coin 10 times and got 7 heads: "So is the chance of heads 7/10 now? I thought it was 1/2!"
teach.praise: 7/10 is the experimental probability from your 10 trials. With many more tosses it should get closer to 1/2. Clever!
teach.nudge: How did you get 7/10? And what might happen if you tossed the coin 1000 times?

learn.hook: A factory cannot test every single pen it makes. So how does it know how many might be faulty? Probability makes the prediction!
points: Expected number of times an event happens = probability × number of trials.
P(not E) = 1 − P(E), because an event either happens or does not.
The probabilities of all the outcomes of an experiment add up to 1.
A prediction is a good estimate, not a promise: the real count may be a little more or less.
A game is fair when every player has the same probability of winning.

example.q: A factory found 3 faulty pens in a sample of 150. About how many faulty pens should it expect in a batch of 2000?

learn.reallife: Insurance companies, doctors and weather forecasters all use probability from past data to plan for the future.

games.title: From least to most likely
games.prompt: Least likely to most likely (one roll of a die or one coin toss)
items: Getting a 7 on a die
Getting a 6 on a die
Getting a head on a coin
Getting a number greater than 1 on a die
Getting a number less than 7 on a die

quiz.q: The probability of rain on any day in July in a town is 0.3. About how many rainy days should you expect in 30 days of July?
quiz.explain: Expected number = 0.3 × 30 = 9 days.
quiz.mistake: Gives the dry days (21) instead of the rainy days

quiz.q: A fair die is rolled 600 times. About how many times would you expect a 4?
quiz.explain: P(4) = 1/6, so the expected number is 1/6 × 600 = 100.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 4 instead of by the 6 faces

quiz.q: If P(E) = 2/7, what is P(not E)?
quiz.mistake: Thinks P(not E) is the reciprocal of P(E)

quiz.q: Joseph hit a six on 12 of the last 60 balls he faced. About how many sixes should he expect in the next 25 balls?
quiz.explain: P(six) = 12/60 = 0.2. Expected sixes = 0.2 × 25 = 5.
quiz.mistake: Uses the old count 12 without scaling to 25 balls

quiz.q: A spinner can stop on A, B or C. P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.3. What is P(C)?
quiz.explain: All probabilities add to 1, so P(C) = 1 − 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2.
quiz.mistake: Adds P(A) and P(B) and stops there

quiz.q: In a game with one die, Riya wins if it shows 6 and Arjun wins if it shows 1 to 5. Is the game fair?
options: No, Arjun's chance is 5/6 and Riya's is only 1/6
Yes, because a die is fair
quiz.explain: A fair game needs equal chances. Arjun has 5 winning outcomes and Riya has just 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a fair die automatically makes any game fair

quiz.q: Arjun tosses a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. What can he conclude?
options: The next toss must be a tail
The coin may still be fair; 10 tosses are too few to be sure
P(head) for this coin is exactly 0.7 forever
quiz.explain: Small samples vary a lot. A fair coin can easily give 7 heads in 10 tosses. Many more tosses are needed to judge.
quiz.mistake: Believes a short run of results proves something, or that a coin 'remembers' past tosses

quiz.q: A bag has 20 marbles. Kabir picks one, notes its colour and puts it back, 100 times. He gets red 30 times. About how many red marbles are in the bag?
quiz.explain: P(red) ≈ 30/100 = 0.3, so about 0.3 × 20 = 6 of the marbles are red.
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of red picks (30) instead of scaling to the 20 marbles

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: "If the chance of rain is 0.3, how many rainy days should I expect in 30 days? And is it guaranteed?"
teach.praise: Multiply 0.3 by 30 to expect about 9 rainy days, but it is an estimate, not a promise. I'll carry an umbrella anyway!
teach.nudge: How do you turn a probability into an expected number? Is the prediction certain?
